title: Graphs and Breadth-First Search
tagline: Learn how a computer finds the route with the fewest edges, before the topic comes up in the COS212 lecture.
goal: Arrive at the COS212 graphs lecture able to describe an undirected, unweighted graph and trace breadth-first search on it by hand.
about: Maps, social networks and delivery apps all answer the same kind of question: how are things connected, and what is the quickest way from one to another? Computer scientists answer it with a graph, which is just dots joined by lines.

In this course you work with one small graph, six vertices named A to F, and learn breadth-first search: a method that explores outward one step at a time, like ripples on water. By the end you can trace it by hand and run it in Python.

objectives.text: Describe a graph using the words vertex, edge and neighbour, and spot an isolated vertex.
List the neighbours of any vertex from a picture or a Python adjacency list.
Trace breadth-first search with a queue, showing the queue after every step.
Explain why a vertex is marked as found when it joins the queue.
Find the route with the fewest edges, and identify vertices that can't be reached.
objectives.checked: Route quick check; checks R5 and R6

glossary.meaning: Vertices (dots) joined by edges (lines). It shows how things are connected.
A dot: one thing in the graph, such as A.
A line joining exactly two vertices, such as A–B.
How many edges touch a vertex. C has degree 3.
A vertex with no edges, like F.
Edges have no numbers on them. Every edge counts as one step.
A dictionary from each vertex to the list of its neighbours.
A line: join at the back, served from the front. First in, first out (FIFO).
A pile: the newest item comes off first. Last in, first out (LIFO).
All the vertices the same number of edges from the start.
Marked the moment a vertex joins the queue, so it never joins twice.
Explores outward level by level, using a queue.
The vertex being served when another vertex was found.
The number of edges on a route (not the number of vertices).
No chain of edges leads there from the start.

default_questions: Why is a vertex marked as found when it joins the queue, not when it's served?
What changes if the edges have distances, like kilometres?
How do we search a graph that's in separate pieces?

Watching.head: You've spent most of your time watching.
Watching.body: Most of your time went to the animations.
tips: Pause at each chapter and predict what happens next before you press play.
Sketch graph A–F and colour it in as the animation plays.
Replay “The queue is a line” (Module 3, section 02) before the lecture.
Watching.stretch: Watch one animation and pause at each chapter to predict what comes next.

Listening.head: You've spent most of your time listening.
Listening.body: Most of your time went to the notes read aloud.
tips: Play the notes at 1.25× while you trace BFS on paper.
Use the microphone to explain each step out loud, then compare with the model answer.
Listen to Module 3 once more on the way to class.
Listening.stretch: Press a speaker on the notes and trace along on paper as you listen.

Reading.head: You've spent most of your time reading.
Reading.body: Most of your time went to the written notes.
tips: Rewrite the BFS recipe in your own words in three lines.
Turn the glossary into flashcards and test yourself.
Read the BFS code line by line in the Code lab.
Reading.stretch: Read the notes on screen once without audio, then summarise them in one line.

Trying.head: You've spent most of your time trying things.
Trying.body: Most of your time went to trial and error on the map.
tips: Do a Mixed practice round: every round has a new graph.
When you miss one, say why the wrong answer fails before moving on.
Use Next step in Module 3, section 04, and predict each row first.
Trying.stretch: Spend five minutes in Be the Queue (Module 3, section 06), where it's fine to get it wrong.

Coding.head: You've spent most of your time coding.
Coding.body: Most of your time went to the code labs.
tips: Predict the printed output before you press Run.
Change the start vertex and run it again.
Add a new vertex to the graph dictionary and see what changes.
Coding.stretch: Open a code lab and press Step five times while watching the queue.

Practising.head: You've spent most of your time practising.
Practising.body: Most of your time went to practice questions.
tips: Try the Full quiz: 15 new questions across all modules.
For any miss, press Show me in the lesson and watch that step.
Practise the module you scored lowest on first.
Practising.stretch: Do a practice round straight after an animation.
